reference.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
clinicalPearls: Unicuspid aortic valve is far rarer than bicuspid disease and typically presents with severe stenosis at a younger age, often in the third to fourth decade.

Two morphological subtypes exist: acommissural (dome-shaped orifice with no commissural attachment to the aortic wall) and unicommissural (a single eccentric commissure producing a teardrop or keyhole orifice); the unicommissural type is more common.
On parasternal short-axis echocardiography the orifice looks eccentric and slit-like, and the classic teardrop shape may be evident only in systole, so image carefully at the leaflet tips.
The valve is frequently misdiagnosed as bicuspid; transoesophageal or 3D echocardiography and cardiac CT or MRI improve accurate counting of commissures.
Associated aortopathy with ascending aortic dilatation occurs independently of haemodynamic severity, so serial aortic imaging is warranted.
Coexisting coarctation of the aorta and other left-heart obstructive lesions should be actively excluded.
Infective endocarditis risk is increased on the structurally abnormal valve.
Young patients frequently require surgery, including the Ross procedure, valve repair or replacement, often combined with aortic root or ascending aortic replacement.
reference.pathophysiology: The anomaly arises from failure of separation of the valve cushions during embryogenesis, producing fusion of one or both commissures so that the valve opens through a single eccentric orifice with one functional commissure (unicommissural) or none (acommissural, dome-shaped). The eccentric restrictive orifice generates turbulent transvalvar flow that accelerates leaflet fibrosis and calcification, leading to progressive stenosis, regurgitation, or a mixed lesion. The same developmental disturbance is associated with an intrinsically abnormal aortic wall showing medial degeneration, which predisposes to ascending aortic dilatation and aneurysm irrespective of valve haemodynamics.
additionalDifferentials: Subvalvar (subaortic membrane) or supravalvar aortic stenosis
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with careful short-axis leaflet imaging
Transoesophageal echocardiography to define commissural morphology
Cardiac CT angiography for valve morphology, calcification and aortic dimensions
Cardiac MRI for regurgitant fraction and aortic assessment
Exercise testing in apparently asymptomatic severe stenosis
redFlags: Exertional syncope, angina or heart failure symptoms indicating severe stenosis
Fever, new regurgitant murmur or embolic phenomena suggesting infective endocarditis
Severe aortic regurgitation with left ventricular dilatation or dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Without intervention severe obstruction or regurgitation develops earlier than in bicuspid disease and often requires surgery in young adulthood. Long-term outcome after valve or root surgery is good, but lifelong surveillance for aortopathy and prosthesis-related complications is required.
pitfalls: Mislabelling a unicommissural valve as bicuspid because a fused commissure mimics a raphe
Assessing morphology only in diastole and missing the systolic teardrop orifice
Underestimating stenosis severity when the eccentric orifice lies off-axis to the Doppler beam
